name: Adam Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take calls for a home appliance maker, booking repairs under warranty, so washing machines, fridges, ovens that have given up. The contact centre's on a retail park, next to a furniture warehouse. I diagnose what I can over the phone, book the engineer, and handle the angry ones when the engineer doesn't show. I like the technical side, working out from a noise that it's the drum bearing. What wears me out is being stuck at a desk when I'd rather be fixing the thing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use technology in that day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I use AI every day, at work and at home. The company's tool suggests fault codes, and I use a chatbot on my phone to look up repair guides for my side work. At weekends I buy broken washing machines cheap, fix them in a garage I rent, and sell them online. My girlfriend Sofia works at a nursery, and we rent a small flat, so we've got about three weeks of money between us, and the garage eats some of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped but useful, and the people who used it got a bit ahead. At work I'd tell the lads to keep using the fault-code tool. Online I'd probably post a photo of a fixed washing machine and say a robot didn't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine in this one, the job stays and my side work keeps growing. I spend all day booking engineers to fix washing machines, and all weekend fixing washing machines myself in a rented garage. The money's still tight, but I can see a way up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for the steady wage. I'd use the AI tools to list my machines faster and price them better. I'd try to save enough to buy a second-hand van in a year or so, so I can deliver and pick up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, a bit impatient. I'd want to grow faster than my savings let me. That's the only real worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much do you make from the washing machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How much do you make from the washing machines?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Sofia think of the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two or three hundred a month, after parts and the garage rent. Some months nothing, if a machine turns out to be scrap. It's not much, but it's mine.

I'd post a photo of a **fixed washing machine** online.
think: His **job stays** and his side work keeps growing.
Money is still tight, but he can see **a way up**.
do: Keep the job for the **steady wage**.
Use **AI tools** to list and price his machines.
Save for a **second-hand van** within a year.

steps.text: Keep the warranty-line job for its steady wage

Save toward a second-hand van within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance for people who are willing to work. At work I'd tell people to learn the tools or learn a trade. I wouldn't blame the company, it's a business, it has to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think half the warranty line goes, because booking engineers is exactly what software does. The warranty line is going to need fewer people like me, so I'd rather be the man with the spanner than the man booking him. Repairs are hands-on, and robots are slower there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an appliance repair qualification, evenings, to make the side work official. I'd keep using AI at work so I'm one of the last to go. I'd put every spare penny into tools and the van, because that's my way out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, and a bit nervous about money. It's the push I've been waiting for. But with three weeks saved, I can't afford a slow month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put every penny into tools. Isn't that risky with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said you'd put every penny into tools. Isn't that risky with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it is. Sofia would say keep a bit back, and she'd be right. I'd probably compromise, half into the business, half in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fast, but people who can fix things will be needed for a while. At work I'd tell people to learn anything hands-on. I'd say families and churches need to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my desk job goes in 2028, maybe before. The repair side lasts till about 2031, when the robots come. Two years isn't long, but it's long enough to turn a garage full of second-hand washing machines into a proper little business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd go full-time on the repairs as soon as the job went, and use AI for everything else, the listings, the bookings, the accounts. I'd buy a cheap van on credit, which scares me. I'd ask my uncle, who's an electrician, to teach me the electrical side fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and fired up at the same time. Three years isn't long to build something. I'd worry most about what happens after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when robots can fix washing machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What happens after 2031, when robots can fix washing machines?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Sofia feel about the van on credit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Maybe people still want a man they trust in their kitchen, maybe not. I'd try to own the business by then, not just be the hands.

I'd urge **families and churches** to look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and people should use it to learn a skill. At work I'd be telling the younger ones to get a trade. I'd post my progress online, the before-and-after photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one suits me. Five years is enough to get qualified as an appliance engineer and have my own van before anyone sends a robot to fix a dishwasher. Robots for hands-on work come around 2034, so I'd have years running my own van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, start the appliance engineer qualification and keep the job. Year two, buy a second-hand van and start doing repairs as well as refurbished sales. By year three, leave the call centre and go full-time, using AI for the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. It's the plan I'd want anyway, just with a deadline. I'd still worry about money until the van's paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you marry in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you marry in that time?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I'd want to marry Sofia in the next couple of years. I'd want the business steady first. That's how my father did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone willing to work can be ready. At work I'd tell people to start now. With friends I'd say it's a good time to start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best one for me. With ten years I'd want to be the boss of a small repair firm, not an employee hoping the company keeps me. I'd be thirty-seven when AGI comes, and robots on repairs not till 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job for a couple of years while I qualify and build the side business. Then I'd go full-time with a van, and maybe hire a lad to help. I'd use AI to run the bookings and the accounts from the start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and excited. It's a long runway, and I'd use it. The only worry is the usual one, money in the early years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take on staff yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Would you take on staff yourself?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could stop you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One or two, if the work's there. Maybe someone from the call centre who wants to learn. I'd like to give someone the start I never got.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to build a business in a hurry with no savings. What would help is cheap loans for small businesses and fast trade qualifications. Not handouts, just a fair start.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me want. Nobody's going to hand me a future, so I'd rather build one with my own hands while the robots are still learning to hold a screwdriver. That's me, really.

headlineQuote: Nobody's going to hand me a future, so I'd rather build one with my own hands while the robots are still learning to hold a screwdriver.
portrait: Adam is a **27-year-old** warranty-line agent for an appliance maker who uses AI daily.
He rents a flat with his girlfriend Sofia and has about **three weeks** saved.
At weekends he **refurbishes washing machines** in a rented garage for extra money.
He sees every scenario as a push toward his own **repair business**, with AI doing paperwork.
He moves from **uneasy** to alarmed only in AGI by 2028, wanting a fair start, not handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, building a business in a hurry with no savings.
